verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies al-Ḥāqqah as the Day of Resurrection, named from ḥaqq for its indisputable, established reality. Repeating the noun and asking "what is it?" magnifies the event; the interrogative ma is its predicate rather than a pronoun. "What will make you know?" denies full knowledge of its reality. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes this Qur'anic formula, which indicates that understanding has been imparted, from "What do you know?", which indicates withholding.

verses.4: Al-Mizan identifies al-Qāriʿah as the Day of Resurrection, whose cosmic shock gives it the name Catastrophe; using the noun rather than a pronoun magnifies it. The destruction of Thamūd, ʿĀd, Pharaoh, earlier disbelievers, the overturned towns of Lot's people, and Noah's people is not merely historical narrative but an explanation of the event: their denial of it brought their total divine annihilation. The later Trumpet scene supplies another aspect of the same answer.
verses.5: Al-Mizan takes al-ṭāghiyah, translated "the Cry," as the destructive means of Thamūd's ruin: a piercing blast, earthquake, or thunderbolt, as Qur'anic accounts vary in the description. Although some take it as their own transgression, the commentary prefers the former because the surrounding verses enumerate the methods by which communities were destroyed.
verses.6: Al-Mizan glosses ṣarṣar as a fierce, bitterly cold, gusting wind and ʿātiyah as a tyrannical force departing from normal obedience and order. God disposed this gale against ʿĀd for seven unbroken nights and eight days: ḥasūm conveys this successive, decisive severing, and their fallen bodies were like hollow, cast-off palm trunks.

verses.8: Al-Mizan takes bāqiyah to mean any survivor, making the question an idiom for their complete annihilation. Reading it instead as the verbal noun for endurance or what remains fits the context less well.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies Pharaoh as Moses' Pharaoh, those before him as earlier disbelieving nations, and the overturned towns as the towns of Lot's people. Khāṭi'ah is a gerund for wrongdoing or straying from the path of servitude to God.
verses.10: Al-Mizan applies the disobedience to Pharaoh, his predecessors, and Lot's people, while "the messenger" is generic for God's messengers. Rābiyah conveys increase, so the seizing is either exceptionally severe or beyond ordinary expectation.
verses.11: Al-Mizan reads the floating jāriyah as Noah's ark and explains "We carried you" by humanity's unity: the experience of ancestors may be ascribed to their descendants. The carrying became a reminder, while receptive ears are those that grasp and preserve its lesson. God universally guides beings to their proper perfection; human distinction lies in voluntary development of the soul through qualities, acts, and states under revealed law. Hence messengers and scriptures establish the path by which faith and obedience yield enduring happiness, whereas turning away yields eternal misery with the proof complete. God's reminder does not compel remembrance: it completes proof, but remembrance is attributed to the human responder because reward follows that voluntary act. The commentary also judges that outward events influence human actions and that actions can affect outward events.

verses.13: Al-Mizan takes the single Trumpet blast as the second blast, reviving the dead for resurrection and final judgment; its singularity marks God's decisive act, needing no repetition. Earth and mountains are lifted and pulverized in one swift leveling, the Hour is established, and the sky splits in weakness. Angels stand at its sides, while the Throne is borne by eight. The apparent reading makes them angelic bearers, though the verse does not settle that; the whole scene may also show that angels, sky, and Throne become visible to humanity.

verses.18: Al-Mizan interprets exposure as presentation before God: every belief and deed, like goods displayed to a buyer, is uncovered when the unseen becomes witnessed and the hidden manifest. God's sole kingdom, command, judgment, and comprehensive knowledge are eternally true; the Day makes these realities apparent without concealment or doubt.
verses.19: Al-Mizan glosses hā'um as a command to a group meaning "take," with forms varying by gender, number, and the Hijazi, Tamim, Qays, and other dialects; it commands rather than prohibits. The right-hand recipient addresses angels and proudly asks them to read a record that decrees his felicity. The final hāʾ of kitābīyah is a pause-marker, and the verses begin the contrast between the happy and wretched conditions of people on that day.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says the speaker's certain expectation of the account in worldly life led him to trust his Lord and watch his deeds, making his record one of the right hand and felicity. A translator's note adds that this includes following the rightful Imām of one's time.
verses.21: Al-Mizan calls the life pleasant by assigning pleasure to life itself: the recipient dwells in an elevated garden of delights beyond human sense, with qutūf, abundant fruit-clusters, readily reached. Food and drink are the recompense for faith and righteous actions sent ahead in the past days. A translator's note adds following the rightful Imām of one's time.

verses.25: Al-Mizan identifies this as the second class, wretched criminals given their record in the left hand. Confronted with the severe torment they now see, they vainly wish for the impossibility of never receiving the record or knowing their account.

verses.27: Al-Mizan says "it" refers to the first death in worldly life. The speaker wishes that death had ended in annihilation and prevented resurrection, rather than leaving him to face the perpetual torment now before him.
verses.28: Al-Mizan presents the lament of one who treated wealth and authority as safeguards of happiness and neglected his Lord, the truth, and its caller. When all means are cut off, he discovers both powerless. The angels are then commanded to seize and fetter him, thrust him into hell, and bind him in a seventy-cubit chain; the fetter joins hands, feet, and neck, and the chain is a shackle measured by the cubit from elbow to fingertip.

verses.33: Al-Mizan grounds the command to seize and chain the sinner in his lack of faith and refusal even to urge feeding the needy, exposing indifference to their suffering. He consequently has no ḥamīm, an intimate friend who can help him: a disbeliever receives neither forgiveness nor intercession on that Day. His food is the bodily discharge of hell's inhabitants, fitting his failure to encourage feeding; only those immersed in sin eat it. Ibn Jarīr reports from Ibn Zayd that the Prophet said four bear the Throne now and eight on the Day; the commentary says "that day" establishes the latter number's specificity. Tafsīr al-Qummī reports eight bearers, four former prophets and Muḥammad, ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn; the author adds reports that the Throne signifies knowledge. In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, Imām al-Ṣādiq links right-hand records to confirmation of the rightful leader, and the author calls reports applying the two hands to ʿAlī, his followers, and enemies applications preceding ordinary exegesis. Al-Durr al-manthūr reports through Abū Saʿīd the unbearable stench of this discharge; it also reports ʿAlī's linguistic response to a Bedouin. Tafsīr al-Burhān reports from the Prophet that even an arm's length of the chain would melt the world's mountains.

verses.38: Al-Mizan reads the oath by what is seen and unseen as encompassing all creation, but excluding God's transcendent Essence: Qur'anic reverence does not place Creator and creation together in one glorification. The oath honors creation's dignity and beauty, which reflect the God who creates only beauty; apparent ugliness arises from creatures themselves and relative comparison. The universe's coherent order displays divine unity and return to God, grounding messengers, scriptures, and the Qur'an's guidance; narrower pairings of seen and unseen are therefore rejected. The noble messenger is Muḥammad, not Gabriel: as a messenger he conveys the Sender's revelation, and the following threat against invented speech suits him. The verses categorically deny that the Qur'an is poetry and rebuke a community in which faith is only a minority condition.

verses.42: Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the Qur'an is soothsaying or that Muḥammad received it from jinn as a soothsayer. "Little is the admonition" rebukes their failure to reflect and remember.
verses.43: Al-Mizan says the Qur'an is gradually sent down by the Lord of all worlds, reaffirming that it is divinely bestowed rather than fabricated by the messenger.
verses.44: Al-Mizan defines fabricating speech as inventing it and attributing it to another. The hypothetical threat concerns the genuine messenger Muḥammad: were he to ascribe to God words God had not spoken, God would seize him, destroy him by severing the fatal waṭīn, and leave no one able to protect him. "By the right hand" may mean gripping a culprit, cutting the hand, or punishing with might; Tafsīr al-Qummī supplies the latter reading. This warning is not a rule that every false claimant to prophethood must be destroyed in this life, since some have not been; it is tailored to God's authentic messenger.

verses.48: Al-Mizan calls the Qur'an a reminder for the Godwary, disclosing the honor of their piety, the realities of origin and return, and their ranks with God in the hereafter. Such disclosure cannot be fabricated, so it confirms the Qur'an's freedom from falsehood.
verses.49: Al-Mizan reads the verses as foretelling that those who deny the Qur'an will meet their regret on the Day of ultimate remorse.

verses.51: Al-Mizan concludes, like Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah, that the Qur'an's account of the Resurrection is certain truth and commands glorification of the All-supreme Lord, who is above purposeless creation, a world without return, or the nullification of these truths. An appended biographical note identifies ʿAllāmah al-Sayyid Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī as a Tabriz-born descendant of al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī who studied in Najaf under leading Shiʿa scholars, then taught in Qum from 1945 until his death in 1981. It credits his wide training in jurisprudence, philosophy, mathematics, and spirituality, calls al-Mīzān his Qur'an-with-Qur'an magnum opus, and notes his further writings and influential students.
